verdicts.reason: Sensorimotor adaptation to ship motion and the readaptation on land are well described; the claim is hedged at the right level and teaches a real mechanism.

"in a way standing still never can" is an absolute nobody measured, and the underlying claim that carrying a tray trains balance is asserted, not evidenced. Drop the absolute and state it as a plausible difference in demand, not a training effect.

Safety: a single-leg stand at a bathroom sink, on a hard and often wet floor, is suggested to an audience that includes seniors, with no mention of keeping a hand near the counter and no naming of the fall risk. Also frames it as "two minutes of practice" when nobody balances on one foot for the full two minutes.
Postural control continues maturing well past toddlerhood into adolescence. True, correctly unquantified, and useful for a young reader.
Symmetric loading keeps the centre of mass closer to the base of support; a one-sided load forces trunk compensation. True at this level of detail, no overclaim.
Plantar cutaneous feedback is a genuine contributor to postural control, and the item hedges honestly ("part of why", "feels steadier") rather than claiming barefoot is measurably better.
Age-related decline in balance is well established; the second clause is an explicit value judgement about spending a minute, not a dose or sufficiency claim.
Single-support phase of gait is real and this reframes something familiar without overstating it.

Firmness. "Most of the tightness" is a proportion nobody measured, and the mechanism is actively argued: current reviews find both reduced passive stiffness and increased stretch tolerance contribute, with tolerance dominant only over longer training periods. Either hedge ("a lot of what you feel is...") or mark contested and say the question is open.

Two defects. It opens with "That's why", a dangling referent to SF-FCT-000190 that breaks when the item is served on its own, which is how this library is read. And "your body has decided the position is safe" is a vivid causal mechanism stated as fact for an acute effect whose cause is not settled.
Hamstrings are biarticular and hip/knee position genuinely changes what a forward bend loads. Accurate and explanatory.

"a lot of why" is an unmeasured proportion, and "shortened position" is the weakest-supported version of this claim. Evidence supports increased passive hip-flexor stiffness and reduced hip extension after prolonged sitting, not structural shortening; no study links length of sitting to hip flexor tightness directly. Rewrite as stiffness, and drop the proportion.
Correct contrast between a multiaxial and a uniaxial joint, and the "on purpose" framing teaches the trade-off rather than just naming parts.
The glenohumeral joint being the most mobile joint in the body is standard anatomy, and the mobility/stability trade-off is correctly stated.

Both halves are wrong in a safety-relevant direction. Ballistic stretching is discouraged primarily for injury risk, not merely because it is "less controlled", and the item explicitly downplays that. And "the range you gain looks much the same either way" is contradicted: meta-analytic comparisons put ballistic stretching's effect on range of motion below static and PNF. Telling a nine-year-old that bouncing gets the same result is the opposite of the guideline.
Individual variation in connective tissue and joint laxity is real, and "some people" keeps it appropriately unquantified. Also usefully defuses comparison between bodies.

The exhale-lets-you-sink-further claim is gym folklore stated as fact ("usually"), with no good evidence behind it, and "Holding your breath does the opposite" invents a matching effect. It also introduces breath-holding as a technique to a nine-year-old audience, which the safety rules avoid. Cut the breath-holding half or reframe the whole item as relaxation, not range.
This is the mainstream warm-up recommendation (ACSM and reviews of acute stretching effects): dynamic movement before activity, static afterwards. The comparative is earned.
Distinguishing stretch tension from sharp pain is exactly the right safety cue for this audience, and it is stated without diagnosing anything.
Accurate description of segmental spinal motion summing to gross range. Teaches something a reader will not have pictured.
Verified: the Achilles is described in the anatomical literature as the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed from gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the calcaneus.
Pandiculation is a real, widely observed vertebrate behaviour and naming it is worth the reader's attention. The "old enough to have its own name" line is a loose flourish but makes no health claim.
Latissimus dorsi runs from the humerus to the thoracolumbar fascia and lower spine, so an overhead reach does load far more than the arm. Accurate.
Accurate description of psoas major, correctly left unnamed for a nine-year-old, and the length of the muscle is genuinely surprising.

"almost nothing" is an overstatement and it contradicts SF-FCT-000197 in this same packet: generalised connective-tissue laxity is precisely why hypermobility is scored across multiple joints. Joint specificity is real; the strength of the claim is not. Soften to "tell you less than you would think".

"the same mechanism" is an unearned identity claim between two practices that have not been shown to work identically, and what follows the colon is a description of practice (regular time at end range), not a mechanism. Restate as "work the same way in practice" or cut the mechanism framing.

Quality failure. It restates SF-FCT-000203 with the content removed and teaches nothing checkable; "one your body asked for on its own" is a phrase, not a fact. Either fold into the pandiculation item or give it real content.

Anatomically wrong: the ankle (talocrural) joint is classified as a uniaxial hinge, the same category as the knee and elbow; the side-to-side motion comes from the subtalar joint below it. "universal joints" is also not a standard classification for the wrist, which is condyloid. And "can't possibly suit all of them" is an overclaim on top of the error.

Stated more firmly than the neuroscience supports. The clean prefrontal-to-striatum handoff is the old account; current work finds both systems remain active and compete rather than one replacing the other, and cortical involvement is task-dependent. "stops needing willpower" also overstates automaticity. Should be hedged or marked contested.

Two proportions nobody measured: "nearly always" and "Most people feel better a few minutes in". There is real work on people mispredicting how exercise will feel, but not at this firmness. Label editorial or hedge to "often".

An absolute and a superlative in one sentence. "Every habit needs a cue" is stated as a law, and "the most reliable cue is" ranks cue types against each other on no measurement — existing-routine anchoring is supported as effective, not as most reliable.
Implementation intentions are among the better-replicated findings in this area, and "noticeably more likely" is hedged correctly rather than quoting an effect size the item cannot source.

"beats" is a head-to-head comparative between two approaches that have not been compared head to head. It is also advice, not a simplified fact, so the confidence label is wrong — SF-FCT-000220 shows `editorial` is available and unused here.

Misstates the peak-end rule: it is peak AND end that dominate retrospective evaluation, and this item drops the peak entirely. "is what pulls you back" then asserts a single cause for return behaviour that the evidence supports only as one predictor among several.

"far more" is an unmeasured comparative. The defensible version — missing a single day does not derail habit formation — is worth saying, but not with a magnitude attached, and this is editorial rather than simplified.

"Streaks work because" asserts a mechanism for the app's own core feature with nothing behind it, and picks one explanation (visibility) over the more obvious ones (loss aversion, commitment). Either hedge to "part of why streaks work" or mark it editorial and own it as a product opinion.

The reactivity of self-monitoring is a real effect, but "purely because you're now paying attention to it" is a mechanism overclaim — tracking also changes what people choose to do because they know it will be recorded. Drop "purely".

"usually physical" is an unmeasured proportion and is likely wrong: the barriers people report most are time, fatigue and how they expect it to feel, not where the shoes are. The examples are good; the ranking claim is not earned.

Honestly labelled `editorial`, which is the right call for a claim like this, and it is safe, plausible and consistent with work on accountability and commitment. The only item in the packet whose confidence field is doing real work.
"holds up better" is presented as a finding but is a comparative nobody measured. Cue consistency is supported in general; time-of-day versus mood specifically is not. Hedge or relabel editorial.
Plainly advice in advice voice, sound, safe, and consistent with the implementation-intention literature without claiming to be a measurement.
Reward immediacy is a well-supported principle of learning, and "stick best" here refers to a genuine and large timing effect rather than an invented ranking.

"The clearest sign" is an unearned superlative. Reduced conscious deliberation and a sense of oddity when skipping are indicators of automaticity, but nothing establishes this as the clearest one. "A good sign" fixes it.
A clean, safe framing that moves attention from outcome goals to today's action, with no empirical claim to overstate.
"faster than changing your mind does" is a speed comparison between two things never measured against each other. The environment-shapes-behaviour point survives without the race.
